newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nuclear firm in fresh turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Japan nuclear firm in fresh turmoil.

text.p: Japan's state-run nuclear company, threatened with break-up after a string of problems, admitted on Thursday it had failed to report 11 radiation leaks at a plant where a new mishap occurred this week.

Officials of the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC), which has been forced to shut down four of its six main facilities, said they failed to report the 11 leaks at an advanced thermal reactor called Fugen in the past three years.
The latest news of problems at Fugen followed a delayed report on Tuesday about a leak of radioactive tritium there that exposed 11 workers to small doses of radiation.
Fugen, located on the coast of the Sea of Japan some 350 km (220 miles) west of Tokyo, is Japan's only reactor to run on heavy water.

PNC officials said they did not report the past accidents because the amount of leaked radiation was below the level at which they were legally required to do so. Local government officials said the PNC should have reported the accidents anyway, in accordance with a prior agreement.

The PNC's latest reports of Fugen accidents followed its admission last week that it had falsified a report about an explosion at its nuclear fuel reprocessing plant at Tokaimura, on the Pacific coast just 100 km (65 miles) northeast of Tokyo.
The March 11 explosion, Japan's worst nuclear accident, exposed 37 workers to low levels of radiation.

Police on Thursday began questioning PNC officials about the doctored report on the Tokaimura explosion after the government's Science and Technology Agency took the rare step of filing a criminal complaint against the firm.
Last week, the PNC admitted its officials had falsified the report, incorrectly saying staff had visually confirmed that a fire had been extinguished at a nuclear waste facility.
In fact, no staff had confirmed that the fire had been put out. The fire later flared up and triggered the explosion.
On Tuesday, the government ordered Fugen shut down, bringing to four the number of the PNC's main facilities to have been deactivated following accidents.

Monju, the PNC's experimental fast-breeder reactor, has been shut down since December 1995 after a massive coolant leak. The Monju case was the first time the PNC had admitted a cover-up, and a PNC official committed suicide over the affair.

The PNC's plutonium fuel production plant has been shut since March 17, when an alarm indicating the reaching of critical mass -- the point at which a nuclear chain reaction begins -- went off in error. The Tokaimura fuel reprocessing plant has also been shut.
The PNC's two other main facilities still in operation are a uranium enrichment plant in Okayama, western Japan, and another experimental fast-breeder reactor called Joyo in Oarai, near Tokaimura.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and senior government officials have expressed exasperation at the PNC's repeated admissions of cover-ups and delays in reporting accidents and have publicly called for some form of disbandment.
"We must re-mould this institution after a thorough investigation," Hashimoto told reporters on Wednesday before the reports on the 11 past Fugen accidents emerged.
"There may be no other way out except for some kind of dismantlement of the PNC," chief government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said.
Science and Technology Minister Riichiro Chikaoka said he was contemplating shutting down all of PNC's facilities. "The PNC has no understanding of public interest," he told reporters.
"If there is no improvement, we may have to order a complete stoppage of all of its operations to establish a speedy and accurate system of accident notification."

The state-run firm is at the heart of Japan's ambitions to boost electricity output from nuclear plants to 42 percent of total power needs by 2010. Nuclear plants now supply one-third of Japan's total power output.
